General Organization of the Central Nervous System

A rostral-to-caudal map of the nervous system: how the CNS and PNS are built, how the brain is protected and subdivided, and how the spinal cord continues the plan below the foramen magnum — built for rapid review before Batch 44's systematic neuroanatomy sequence.

Lecture created by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen Batch 44 · Neuroscience 17 sections · 26 figures · quiz + flashcards

Course Roadmap

This lecture lays the scaffolding for everything that follows in the systematic neuroanatomy series. It is intentionally a broad overview — later lectures return to each structure (cranial nerve nuclei, the brainstem, the limbic system, the ventricular system) in full detail.

Learning objectives

  • State the two major divisions of the nervous system and the components of each.
  • List the 12 pairs of cranial nerves and the 31 pairs of spinal nerves, with their regional breakdown.
  • Differentiate a ganglion from a nucleus.
  • Describe the location, protective mechanisms, gross parts, and internal structure of the brain.
  • Describe the location, vertebral level of termination, protection, segmental parts, and internal structure of the spinal cord.

Key concepts at a glance

  • CNS = brain + spinal cord.
  • PNS = cranial nerves + spinal nerves + associated ganglia.
  • Brain organization: outer grey matter (cortex), inner white matter, with grey nuclei embedded deep inside.
  • Spinal cord organization is the mirror image: inner grey matter, outer white matter.
  • Three shared protective layers for both brain and cord: bone, meninges, CSF.
⭐⭐⭐ Must Know A ganglion is a collection of neuronal cell bodies outside the CNS; a nucleus is a collection of neuronal cell bodies inside the CNS. This distinction is used throughout neuroanatomy and is a favourite viva question.

CNS & PNS — The Two Divisions

The nervous system is divided into two major components, each built from further sub-components.

1) Central Nervous System (CNS)

  • Brain
  • Spinal cord

2) Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

  • Cranial nerves — 12 pairs, arise from / terminate in the brain
  • Peripheral (spinal) nerves — 31 pairs, arise from the spinal cord
  • Associated ganglia — collections of neuronal cell bodies outside the CNS

Cranial Nerves (CN I–XII)

Twelve paired nerves, numbered by their order of attachment to the brain (from anterior/superior to posterior/inferior). Two (CN I and CN II) terminate directly in the brain rather than truly "arising" from it; the remaining ten emerge from the brain itself. CN VIII arises instead from the inner ear and terminates in the brain.

No.NameModalityKey note
IOlfactorySpecial sensoryFibres from the olfactory area of the nasal cavity (lateral wall & septum) form the olfactory bulb, which continues as the olfactory tract, terminating in the brain.
IIOpticSpecial sensoryRuns from the eye to the occipital lobe (visual area).
IIIOculomotorMixedArises from the brain.
IVTrochlearMotorArises from the brain.
VTrigeminalMixedArises from the brain.
VIAbducensMotorArises from the brain.
VIIFacialMixedArises from the brain.
VIIIVestibulocochlear (Auditory / Statoacoustic)Special sensoryTwo parts: vestibular (balance) and cochlear (hearing). Arises from the inner ear and terminates in the brain.
IXGlossopharyngealMixedArises from the brain.
XVagus ("the wanderer")MixedThe only cranial nerve that leaves the neck to enter the thorax, then travels to the abdomen, terminating in the distal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
XISpinal accessoryMotorTwo components — a cranial root (from the brainstem) and a spinal root (from the neck/upper cervical cord) — that join to form a single nerve.
XIIHypoglossalPure motorSupplies the muscles of the tongue. Being pure motor, it has no associated ganglia.
⭐⭐ High Yield Cranial nerves are grouped as mixed (carry both motor and sensory fibres, e.g. facial, vagus) or pure (one modality only, e.g. hypoglossal — pure motor). Nerves that carry a sensory component have associated ganglia; a pure motor nerve such as CN XII does not.
🩺 Clinical Pearl Vagus nerve trajectory: because CN X extends far beyond the cranial cavity into the thorax and abdomen, understanding its course is essential for localising symptoms that span multiple organ systems — e.g. heart-rate regulation and gastrointestinal motility.

Spinal Nerves & Associated Ganglia

The second component of the PNS is the peripheral (spinal) nerves, which arise from the spinal cord.

31 pairs total

8 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 sacral · 1 coccygeal

Origin

All 31 pairs arise from the spinal cord.

Ganglia

Every spinal nerve has an associated dorsal root ganglion.

Ganglion vs. Nucleus

GanglionNucleus
DefinitionCollection of neuronal cell bodiesCollection of neuronal cell bodies
LocationOutside the CNSInside the CNS
ExampleDorsal root ganglion of a spinal nerveA thalamic or hypothalamic nucleus

The Brain — Overview

The brain is studied under four headings: location, protection, parts, and structure.

1. Location

The brain is located in the cranial cavity, within the skull. The body contains four major cavities:

Cranial cavity

Contains the brain

Thoracic cavity

Contains the lungs, heart, great blood vessels, oesophagus, pharynx

Abdominal cavity

Abdominal viscera

Pelvic cavity

Pelvic viscera

2. Protection

The CNS (brain and spinal cord) is protected by three mechanisms:

  1. Bony protection — the skull (for the brain) / the vertebral column (for the spinal cord).
  2. Meninges — a system of three membranes: dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater.
  3. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) — occupies the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and pia mater, and suspends the brain within it.

The three meninges

  • Dura mater — outermost, tough; has two layers (periosteal layer, adherent to the inner skull surface, and the meningeal layer).
  • Arachnoid mater — middle layer, a single layer.
  • Pia mater — innermost, closely adherent to the brain surface, a single layer.

Falx cerebri

A fold of the meningeal layer of the dura mater that projects into the longitudinal fissure between the two cerebral hemispheres, supporting the brain. Within it run dural venous sinuses (veins draining the brain, distinct from the veins that run within brain tissue).

⭐⭐⭐ Must Know Three protective mechanisms for the brain: the skull, the meninges, and the CSF (in the subarachnoid space). The same three principles (bone, meninges, CSF) protect the spinal cord — substituting the vertebral column for the skull.
🩺 Clinical Pearl A disruption of any one of these three mechanisms — a skull fracture, meningitis (infection/inflammation of the meninges), or a subarachnoid haemorrhage (bleeding into the CSF-filled space) — directly threatens the CNS.

3. Parts

The brain is divided into three parts:

Forebrain

Cerebrum + Diencephalon

Midbrain

A single small connecting part

Hindbrain

Cerebellum + Pons + Medulla oblongata

Cerebrum

The largest part of the brain and the first division of the forebrain (the second being the diencephalon).

Gross features

  • Consists of two cerebral hemispheres (right and left), shaped like two half-spheres.
  • The hemispheres are connected by a mass of white matter, the corpus callosum — the largest of several inter-hemispheric connections (others include the anterior commissure, posterior commissure, and habenular commissure).
  • The hemispheres are separated by a deep cleft, the longitudinal fissure, into which the falx cerebri projects.

External features: gyri, sulci, and the lobes

  • The surface layer of each hemisphere, the cortex, is composed of grey matter.
  • The cerebral cortex is not smooth — it is thrown into folds, or gyri, separated by grooves, the sulci (or fissures).
  • A number of large sulci are used to subdivide the surface of each hemisphere into four lobes.
Major sulcusDivides / borders
Central sulcusSeparates the frontal lobe (anterior) from the parietal lobe (posterior)
Lateral (Sylvian) fissureSeparates the temporal lobe (below) from the frontal/parietal lobes (above)
Parieto-occipital sulcusSeparates the parietal lobe (anterior) from the occipital lobe (posterior)
LobeBoundary
Frontal lobeAnterior to the central sulcus
Parietal lobeBetween the central sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus
Occipital lobePosterior to the parieto-occipital sulcus
Temporal lobeInferior to the lateral fissure
🩺 Clinical Pearl — Lesion localisation Knowing the boundaries of the cerebral lobes is vital for localising clinical deficits. A lesion anterior to the central sulcus (frontal lobe) tends to present with motor/executive dysfunction, while a lesion posterior to it (parietal lobe) tends to present with sensory dysfunction.

Structure of the Cerebrum & Basal Nuclei

Internally, each cerebral hemisphere is organised opposite to the way it looks from outside: grey cortex on the surface, white matter beneath — and, deep within that white matter, further islands of grey matter.

Internal architecture of the hemisphere

  • Outer cortex — grey matter.
  • Deep to the cortex, a central core of white matter.
  • Within that white matter, large masses of grey matter form the basal nuclei, commonly (if imprecisely) called the basal ganglia.

Note: unlike an organ such as the adrenal gland (which has a true cortex and medulla), the brain has no "medulla" in this sense — only a grey cortex outside and white matter inside, containing embedded grey nuclei.

The three basal nuclei

NucleusDescription
Lentiform nucleusLens-shaped mass of grey matter.
Caudate nucleusElongated, "tail-like" (worm-shaped) nucleus; its tail curves round to end near the amygdaloid nucleus.
Amygdaloid nucleus (amygdaloid body)Sits at the end of the tail of the caudate nucleus.

Each cerebral hemisphere contains this trio of basal nuclei, embedded within its white matter.

⭐⭐ High Yield The technically correct term is basal nuclei (they lie inside the CNS, so by definition cannot be a true "ganglion"), but basal ganglia remains the conventional, widely used name.

Diencephalon

The second division of the forebrain and its central part, entirely composed of grey matter (nuclei), apart from the white matter of the corpus callosum which is not itself part of the diencephalon.

Thalamus

Superior division

Hypothalamus

Inferior division

Subthalamus

Lies just above the midbrain

Epithalamus

Uppermost, near the pineal body

Epi- = above, sub- = below, hypo- = under — the prefixes describe each part's position relative to the thalamus.

Thalamus

A large, egg-shaped mass of grey matter that lies on either side of the third ventricle, forming most of its lateral wall. Composed of multiple nuclei (e.g. ventral posterior, ventral anterior, paraventricular nuclei), mirrored on the right and left sides.

Hypothalamus

Forms the lower part of the lateral wall and floor of the third ventricle, lying immediately below the thalamus. Composed of nuclei (e.g. anterior, posterior, and lateral hypothalamic nuclei). Intimately related to the pituitary gland, which it regulates — making the hypothalamus the master controller of the body's endocrine system.

The third ventricle

A midline slit-like cavity between the right and left thalamus/hypothalamus, whose lateral wall and floor are formed by the thalamus and hypothalamus respectively. The brain contains four ventricles in total: two lateral ventricles (one within each cerebral hemisphere), the third ventricle, and the fourth ventricle.

🩺 Clinical Pearl The hypothalamus–pituitary relationship is functionally and physically intimate: the hypothalamus serves as the master regulator of the endocrine system via its control of the pituitary gland.

Midbrain

The narrow, connecting segment of the brain — small in size but functionally dense.

  • Connects the forebrain to the hindbrain.
  • Contains numerous nuclei.
  • Contains bundles of ascending and descending nerve fibre tracts.
Tract directionCarries
Ascending tractsSensory information travelling up to the brain
Descending tractsMotor commands travelling down from the brain
⭐⭐ High Yield Distinguishing ascending (sensory) from descending (motor) tracts is essential for localising sensory versus motor deficits along the neuraxis.

Hindbrain

The third and most caudal division of the brain, comprising three parts.

Pons

Part of the brainstem

Medulla oblongata

Part of the brainstem; continues as the spinal cord

Cerebellum

Lies posterior to the pons/medulla

  • The pons and medulla oblongata together form part of the brainstem.
  • The cerebellum sits posterior to the brainstem; its principal function is coordination of movement and balance.
  • The medulla oblongata terminates at the foramen magnum, where it becomes continuous with the spinal cord.

The Spinal Cord

Studied under five headings: location, beginning and termination, protection, parts, and structure.

1. Location

Located within the vertebral column, inside the vertebral canal — the canal formed by the stacked vertebral foramina of successive vertebrae.

2. Beginning & Termination

  • Begins superiorly at the foramen magnum in the skull, where it is continuous with the medulla oblongata of the brain.
  • Terminates inferiorly in the lumbar region, not extending beyond the lower border of L2.
🩺 Clinical Pearl — Lumbar puncture Knowing that the spinal cord terminates at the lower border of L2 is a critical landmark for performing a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) safely, below this level, to avoid injuring the cord itself.

3. Protection

  • Vertebral column — bony protection, housing the cord in the vertebral canal.
  • Three meninges — dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater (the same layers that protect the brain).
  • Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) — further protection, occupying the subarachnoid space around the cord (continuous with the CSF around the brain).

4. Parts (Segments)

The spinal cord is divided into segments, named according to the vertebral region through which it passes:

Cervical

Thoracic

Lumbar

Sacral

Coccygeal

⭐⭐ High Yield Because the cord ends at L2 while the vertebral column continues further down, the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal segments are compressed together, crowding into the lumbar region rather than extending the full length of their matching vertebrae.

5. Structure

  • The spinal cord is composed of an inner core of grey matter, surrounded by an outer covering of white matter — the exact opposite arrangement to the brain (outer grey cortex, inner white matter).
  • On cross-section, the grey matter forms an H-shaped pillar, with anterior and posterior grey columns (horns), joined by a thin grey commissure that contains the small central canal.
  • The white matter is divided into anterior, lateral, and posterior white columns (funiculi).
⭐⭐⭐ Must Know Brain: grey matter outside (cortex), white matter inside, with grey nuclei embedded deep within.
Spinal cord: white matter outside, H-shaped grey matter inside.

Memory & Mnemonics

Quick recall aids for the highest-yield lists in this lecture.

"On Old Olympus' Towering Top, A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops"

Cranial nerves I–XII, in order: Olfactory, Optic, Oculomotor, Trochlear, Trigeminal, Abducens, Facial, Vestibulocochlear (Auditory), Glossopharyngeal, Vagus, (Spinal) Accessory, Hypoglossal.

"Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More"

Sensory / Motor / Both for CN I–XII: Sensory (I, II, VIII), Motor (III, IV, VI, XI, XII), Both/mixed (V, VII, IX, X).

Ganglion = "G is for Going out" — leaves the CNS

Ganglion vs. nucleus: a ganglion is a cell-body collection that has "gone out" of the CNS; a nucleus stays "in" the CNS.

"CHiTLS" from top to bottom

Diencephalon parts, superior → inferior: Epithalamus, Thalamus, Subthalamus, Hypothalamus — remember by the prefixes: epi- (above), sub- (just below thalamus), hypo- (further below).

"8-12-5-5-1"

Spinal nerve count by region: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal = 31 pairs total.

Brain = "grey coat, white core"  |  Cord = "white coat, grey core"

Grey/white matter arrangement: the brain's cortex is grey with white matter inside; the spinal cord is the reverse — white matter outside, grey matter (H-shaped) inside.

Glossary — Difficult Vocabulary

Key terms introduced in this lecture.

Gyrus / Gyri
A fold (or folds) of the cerebral cortex, raised above the surrounding surface.
Sulcus / Sulci (fissure)
A groove of the cerebral cortex, lying between adjacent gyri.
Falx cerebri
A sickle-shaped fold of the meningeal layer of the dura mater that projects into the longitudinal fissure between the cerebral hemispheres.
Dural venous sinuses
Venous channels running within the dural folds (e.g. the falx cerebri) that drain blood from the brain.
Corpus callosum
The largest band of white matter connecting the right and left cerebral hemispheres.
Commissure
A bundle of nerve fibres crossing the midline, connecting corresponding areas of the two hemispheres (e.g. corpus callosum, anterior/posterior/habenular commissures).
Meninges
The three connective-tissue membranes (dura, arachnoid, pia mater) that envelop the brain and spinal cord.
Subarachnoid space
The space between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, containing cerebrospinal fluid.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
The fluid occupying the subarachnoid space and the ventricular system, cushioning and supporting the brain and spinal cord.
Foramen magnum
The large opening in the base of the skull through which the medulla oblongata becomes continuous with the spinal cord.
Vertebral canal
The canal formed by the aligned vertebral foramina of the stacked vertebrae, housing the spinal cord.
Basal nuclei (basal ganglia)
Masses of grey matter (lentiform, caudate, amygdaloid nuclei) embedded deep within the white matter of each cerebral hemisphere.
Third ventricle
The narrow, midline cavity of the diencephalon, bordered laterally by the thalamus and hypothalamus.
Brainstem
The stalk-like part of the brain formed by the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata, connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord.
Ascending / descending tracts
Bundles of nerve fibres carrying, respectively, sensory information up to the brain and motor commands down from the brain.
Grey / white column (horn)
In the spinal cord, projections of grey matter (anterior and posterior) seen on cross-section, forming the limbs of the characteristic H shape.
Grey commissure
The thin bridge of grey matter joining the two sides of the spinal cord's H-shaped grey matter, containing the central canal.

🚨 High-Yield Exam Zone

Every high-yield and clinical pearl from the lecture, gathered in one place for last-minute review.

⭐⭐⭐ Must-Know Facts

  • The CNS comprises the brain and spinal cord.
  • There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves (Olfactory, Optic, Oculomotor, Trochlear, Trigeminal, Abducens, Facial, Vestibulocochlear, Glossopharyngeal, Vagus, Spinal Accessory, Hypoglossal).
  • The vagus nerve (CN X) is the only cranial nerve that leaves the neck to innervate the thorax and abdomen, terminating in the distal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
  • The spinal nerves total 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal.
  • A ganglion is a collection of neuronal cell bodies outside the CNS; a nucleus is a collection of neuronal cell bodies inside the CNS.
  • The brain is protected by three mechanisms: the skull, the meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia mater), and the CSF in the subarachnoid space.
  • The brain divides into the forebrain (cerebrum + diencephalon), midbrain, and hindbrain (cerebellum, pons, medulla oblongata).
  • The two cerebral hemispheres are joined mainly by the corpus callosum.
  • The cerebral surface (cortex) is grey matter, folded into gyri separated by sulci/fissures.
  • Large sulci (lateral, central, parieto-occipital) divide the cerebrum into four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital.
  • The correct term for the deep grey matter of the hemispheres is basal nuclei (lentiform, caudate, amygdaloid), though commonly called basal ganglia.
  • Spinal cord segments (lumbar through coccygeal) do not extend beyond the lower border of L2.
  • The diencephalon has exactly four parts: thalamus, hypothalamus, subthalamus, epithalamus.
  • The brain's structural arrangement (outer grey / inner white) is the exact opposite of the spinal cord's (outer white / inner grey).

🩺 Clinical Pearls

  • The vagus nerve's long course beyond the cranial cavity is key to localising symptoms across the heart and gastrointestinal tract.
  • A disruption of the skull, meninges, or CSF (skull fracture, meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage) directly threatens the CNS.
  • The central sulcus is a key landmark: lesions anterior to it (frontal lobe) tend to be motor/executive; lesions posterior to it (parietal lobe) tend to be sensory.
  • The hypothalamus–pituitary axis is the master controller of the body's endocrine system.
  • The spinal cord's termination at the lower border of L2 is the critical landmark for safely performing a lumbar puncture below this level.
  • Ascending tracts carry sensory information; descending tracts carry motor commands — essential for localising sensory vs. motor deficits.

Spotter / Viva Prompts

  • Identify the structure joining the two cerebral hemispheres on a coronal section. ⭐⭐
  • Name the only cranial nerve to leave the neck and enter the abdomen. ⭐⭐⭐
  • On a labelled lateral view, identify the sulcus separating the frontal and parietal lobes. ⭐⭐
  • Differentiate a ganglion from a nucleus with one example each. ⭐⭐⭐
  • State the vertebral level at which the spinal cord terminates and its clinical significance. ⭐⭐⭐
  • List the three meninges from outermost to innermost. ⭐
